slides.title: Demand Forecasting
slides.text:
Demand Forecasting
Demand forecasting is the process of estimating the future demand for a product or service using historical data, market information, and/or statistical and judgmental methods.

bullets.text: Demand forecasting is the process of estimating the future demand for a product or service using historical data, market information, and/or statistical and judgmental methods.

slides.title: Decisions that Need Forecasts
slides.text:
Decisions that Need Forecasts
Which markets to pursue?
What products to produce?
How many people to hire?
How many inputs to purchase?
How many units to produce?
The forecast is a bridge between uncertainty about the future and today's business decisions

slides.text:
Common Characteristics of Forecasting
Forecasts are rarely perfect
Can we make the forecast sufficiently accurate to make better decisions?
Forecasts are more accurate for aggregated data than for individual items
Forecast are more accurate for shorter than longer time periods

Market research/Consumer surveys: uses surveys and interviews to identify customer preferences; good determinant of customer preferences; it can be difficult to develop a good questionnaire. Executive opinion: a group of managers meet and come up with a forecast; good for strategic or new-product forecasting; one person's opinion can dominate the forecast. Delphi method: seeks to develop a consensus among a group of experts; excellent for forecasting long-term product demand, technological; time consuming to develop.

Trend
Seasonality
Cycle
slides.visual_text: Composition of Time Series Data. Data = historic pattern + random variation. Historic pattern may include level (long-term average), trend, seasonality and cycle.

slides.title: Time Series Patterns
slides.text: Time Series Patterns
slides.visual_text: Four small graphs of quantity against time titled Time Series Patterns. (a) Level or horizontal pattern: data follows a horizontal pattern around the mean. (b) Trend pattern: data is progressively increasing (shown) or decreasing. (c) Seasonal pattern: data exhibits a regularly repeating pattern, shown over quarters 1 to 4 repeating. (d) Cycle: data increases or decreases over time, a slow wave over several years of quarters.

slides.title: Smoothing Approaches
slides.text:
Smoothing Approaches
When we forecast using historical data, the data contain two things: an underlying pattern and random fluctuations.
Trend forecasting → captures the underlying pattern.
If we fit a trend line, we are imposing a particular mathematical pattern on the data.
But perhaps we don't want to assume that the underlying relationship is necessarily linear or quadratic.
So,
Moving Average → Smooth the data by averaging recent observations.

bullets.text: When we forecast using historical data, the data contain two things: an underlying pattern and random fluctuations.
Trend forecasting → captures the underlying pattern.
If we fit a trend line, we are imposing a particular mathematical pattern on the data.
But perhaps we don't want to assume that the underlying relationship is necessarily linear or quadratic.
Moving Average → Smooth the data by averaging recent observations.

slides.title: Moving Averages Approach
slides.text: Moving Averages Approach
slides.visual_text: Moving Averages Approach. The forecast for the next period is the average of observations from a fixed number of recent periods. For a 3-period moving average: F(t+1) = (Y(t) + Y(t-1) + Y(t-2)) / 3, where Y(t) = actual observation and F(t+1) = forecast for next period. Why use moving average: 1. Smoothens random fluctuations 2. Easy to calculate 3. Uses recent observations.

slides.title: 5-period Moving Average
slides.text: 5-period Moving Average
slides.visual_text: Table titled 5-period Moving Average. Columns: Year, Actual Sales (A), 3-year MA forecast (F), A-F, (A-F)², 5-year MA forecast (F), A-F, (A-F)². 2017 to 2019 have no forecasts. 2020: 100, 85, 15, 225. 2021: 120, 91.67, 28.33, 802.58. 2022: 110, 103.33, 6.67, 44.48, and 5-year 95, 15, 225. 2023: 130, 110, 20, 400, and 101, 29, 841. 2024: 140, 120, 20, 400, and 110, 30, 900. 2025: 150, 126.67, 23.33, 544.28, and 120, 30, 900. Sum of (At - Ft)²: 2416.367 for the 3-year MA and 2866 for the 5-year MA. Forecasts for 2026: 140 (3-year) and 130 (5-year).

slides.title: Choosing between 3- and 5-period Moving Average
slides.text: Choosing between 3- and 5-period Moving Average
slides.visual_text: Choosing between 3- and 5-period Moving Average. Calculate the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) for each and compare; choose the MA that has lower RMSE. RMSE = square root of [Σ(At - Ft)² / n], where n = number of periods for which MA values are available. RMSE3 = √(2416.367 / 6) = 20.068. RMSE5 = √(2866 / 4) = 26.767. Since RMSE3 < RMSE5, the 3-year moving average is selected as the preferred forecasting method. Therefore, the forecast for 2026 is 140 units.

slides.title: Exponential Smoothening Approach
slides.text:
Exponential Smoothening Approach
Moving average has one limitation: It gives equal importance to all observations within the window.
But intuitively, 2025 sales might tell us more about 2026 sales than 2023 sales.
That's where exponential smoothing comes in: Give more importance to recent observations and progressively less importance to older observations.

bullets.text: Moving average has one limitation: It gives equal importance to all observations within the window.
But intuitively, 2025 sales might tell us more about 2026 sales than 2023 sales.
That's where exponential smoothing comes in: Give more importance to recent observations and progressively less importance to older observations.

slides.title: Exponential Smoothening Approach
slides.text: Exponential Smoothening Approach
slides.visual_text: Exponential Smoothening Approach. The basic equation is F(t+1) = αY(t) + (1 - α)F(t), where F(t+1) = forecast for next period, Y(t) = actual value in current period, F(t) = forecast for current period, α = smoothing constant, and 0 < α < 1.

slides.text:
The table below gives actual sales value for period 2020-2024. Suppose α=0.3, find the sales forecast for the year 2025.
Year | Actual sales
2020 | 100
2021 | 120
2022 | 110
2023 | 130
2024 | 140

bullets.text: The table below gives actual sales value for period 2020-2024. Suppose α=0.3, find the sales forecast for the year 2025.

slides.title: Solution
slides.text: Solution
slides.visual_text: Solution. We need an initial forecast. For simplicity, we assume F2021 = 100, that is, we use the first actual observation as the initial forecast. Forecast for 2022: F2022 = αY2021 + (1 - α)F2021 = 0.3 × 120 + (1 - 0.3) × 100 = 36 + 70 = 106. Forecast for 2023: F2023 = 0.3 × 110 + (1 - 0.3) × 106 = 33 + 74.2 = 107.2. Forecast for 2024: F2024 = 0.3 × 130 + (1 - 0.3) × 107.2 = 39 + 75.04 = 114.04. Forecast for 2025: F2025 = 0.3 × 140 + (1 - 0.3) × 114.04 = 42 + 79.828 = 121.83. F2025 = 121.83.
